lessons.title: Currency Regimes: Fixed, Floating and India's Managed Float

children.text: USD/INR moved from about 81 to 83 to 85 over the last few years, drifting a little most weeks. The UAE dirham, meanwhile, has sat at almost exactly 3.6725 per dollar for decades, barely moving at all. Both are real exchange rates for real economies. The difference is not luck, it is a deliberate policy choice each country's central bank makes, called a currency regime, and it shapes almost everything else you will study in this course.

body.text: A currency regime is how much a central bank commits to controlling its exchange rate, ranging from a hard fixed peg at one end to a fully free float at the other. India sits in the middle, a managed float, and understanding why it sits there explains a lot of what the RBI does and does not do.

children.text: The Spectrum: Fixed, Floating and Everything in Between

markDefs.definition: An extreme form of a fixed regime where a central bank holds foreign currency reserves equal to (or greater than) its entire domestic currency in circulation, and is legally committed to exchange one for the other at a fixed rate on demand.

children.text: In a
fixed (or pegged) regime

, the central bank commits to buying and selling its currency at a specific rate against another currency, no matter what market forces say. The UAE dirham and the Saudi riyal have been pegged to the US dollar for decades this way. Hong Kong runs an even stricter version, a
currency board

, where every Hong Kong dollar in circulation is backed by US dollar reserves. The upside is total predictability for trade and investment. The cost is steep: defending the peg during a crisis can burn through a country's entire reserve stockpile, and the central bank effectively gives up the ability to set interest rates independently to manage its own economy.
At the other end sits a
freely floating regime

, where the exchange rate is left almost entirely to supply and demand in the open market. The US dollar, the euro, the British pound and the Japanese yen are the textbook examples: their central banks rarely intervene directly to move the exchange rate, and when they do, it is treated as newsworthy precisely because it is so unusual. A floating currency absorbs economic shocks automatically, a weaker currency cushions an export-led economy during a slowdown, for instance, but it also means day-to-day volatility that businesses and investors simply have to live with.
Most large economies today, including India, sit somewhere in between, in a
managed float

, sometimes called a dirty float. The exchange rate is primarily market-determined day to day, but the central bank steps in periodically to smooth out excessive volatility, not to defend any single fixed level. This is the regime the rest of this course is built around, because it is the one that actually governs the rupee.

body.caption: Fixed, floating and managed float, side by side

cells: Fixed / Pegged

children.text: India's Managed Float: How the RBI Actually Operates

markDefs.definition: Non-Deliverable Forward: a forward contract on a currency pair, traded offshore in centres like Singapore and London, that settles in cash rather than delivering the actual currency. The RBI began intervening in the offshore NDF market for the rupee in 2020.

children.text: The RBI has been explicit that it does not target a specific level for the rupee. Its stated job is to prevent excessive, disorderly volatility, not to hold USD/INR at any particular number. In practice this means the RBI buys dollars when the rupee strengthens too fast, adding to its reserves, and sells dollars from those reserves when the rupee weakens too fast, cushioning the fall. It operates in the spot market directly, in the forward market, and since 2020, in the offshore
NDF
market as well, closing off a channel where large offshore bets on the rupee used to move the onshore rate with the RBI unable to act directly.

body.text: A useful way to tell a managed float from a peg: under a peg, a central bank's interventions are frequent, predictable and aimed at one specific number. Under India's managed float, RBI intervention is irregular, aimed at the pace of movement rather than a level, and openly acknowledged as smoothing, not defending a target.

children.text: Why Regime Choice Matters: The Impossible Trinity

markDefs.definition: Also called the trilemma: the proposition that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital across its borders, and an independent monetary policy. At most two of the three are achievable at once.

children.text: Regime choice is not arbitrary, it is constrained by a well-established idea in international economics called the
impossible trinity

. A country can pick at most two of three things: a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital in and out of the country, and an independent monetary policy set purely for domestic needs. Try to have all three and the system breaks, if capital floods in chasing higher domestic interest rates while the exchange rate is fixed, the central bank either has to let the peg go or abandon its own interest rate decisions to defend it.

body.caption: The impossible trinity: pick any two

cells: Fixed rate + free capital flows
Independent monetary policy
Hong Kong (currency board), Eurozone members
Free capital flows + independent monetary policy
A fixed exchange rate (must float instead)
United States, United Kingdom, Japan
Fixed/managed rate + independent monetary policy
Fully free capital flows (some capital controls remain)
India, China

children.text: India's answer to the trilemma is a managed float paired with an independent, inflation-targeting RBI and only partial capital account convertibility, the current account (trade, remittances, services) has been fully convertible since 1994, but capital account transactions, foreign investment limits, external borrowing rules, still carry restrictions. That combination is exactly why the RBI can run its own interest rate policy to fight domestic inflation without being forced to defend a fixed rupee level at any cost.
A Quick History: How India Got to a Managed Float

body.title: The Rupee's Journey from a Fixed Peg to a Managed Float

events.title: Pegged to the British Pound
events.description: Independent India inherited a rupee fixed to the pound sterling, a colonial-era arrangement carried forward after 1947.

events.title: Peg Shifts to a Currency Basket
events.description: India moved the rupee's peg from the pound alone to a basket of currencies of its major trading partners, reducing dependence on any single currency.

events.title: Balance of Payments Crisis Forces Devaluation
events.description: With foreign exchange reserves critically low, India devalued the rupee in two steps within days, a turning point that opened the door to broader economic liberalisation.

events.title: LERMS: A Dual Exchange Rate System
events.description: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System introduced a partial market-determined rate alongside the official rate, a transitional step toward a fully market-based system.

events.title: Unified, Market-Determined Exchange Rate
events.description: India moved to a single, market-determined exchange rate, the starting point of the managed float regime that continues today.

events.title: Formal Inflation Targeting Begins
events.description: The RBI Act was amended to formally adopt flexible inflation targeting, giving the RBI a clear domestic mandate to run alongside its currency-smoothing role.

body.title: Currency Regime Terms to Lock In

cards.definition: The central bank commits to a specific exchange rate and buys/sells its currency on demand to defend it.
The exchange rate is set almost entirely by market supply and demand, with rare central bank intervention.
A market-determined rate day to day, with the central bank intervening occasionally to smooth volatility, not defend a fixed level. India's regime.
A strict form of a fixed regime where every unit of domestic currency in circulation is backed by foreign reserves, as in Hong Kong.
A country can have at most two of: a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows, and an independent monetary policy, never all three.

How freely a currency can be converted for capital (investment, borrowing) transactions, as opposed to current account items like trade and remittances. India's capital account is only partially convertible.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: The UAE dirham has traded at almost exactly 3.6725 per US dollar for decades, regardless of oil prices, US interest rates or global market swings. Which regime is this?
body.explanation: A rate held at essentially one number for decades, defended regardless of market conditions, is the signature of a fixed or pegged regime, in this case backed by the UAE's central bank commitment to convert dirhams for dollars at that rate on demand.

body.title: Testing the Trilemma
body.scenario: A policymaker proposes that India should simultaneously: (1) fix USD/INR permanently at ₹80, (2) fully open the capital account so foreign money can flow in and out with no restrictions, and (3) keep setting interest rates purely to manage domestic inflation, independent of what any other country does.
body.prompt: Using the impossible trinity, explain why this combination cannot hold. If foreign capital surges into India chasing higher interest rates, what breaks first, the fixed rate, the open capital account, or the RBI's independent rate decisions?
body.modelAnswer: The trilemma says India can keep at most two of the three. If capital flows in freely (open capital account) chasing India's independently-set higher interest rates, that inflow puts upward pressure on the rupee. To hold the rate fixed at ₹80, the RBI would have to intervene by selling rupees or cutting interest rates to reduce the inflow, but cutting rates purely to defend the currency, regardless of what domestic inflation needs, is exactly what "independent monetary policy" means giving up. So the RBI faces a forced choice: either let the fixed rate break (allow the rupee to move), restrict the capital inflow (give up full capital account openness), or subordinate its interest rate decisions to defending ₹80 (give up independent monetary policy). It cannot keep all three; the fixed rate is typically the first thing to give, which is exactly why India runs a managed float rather than a hard peg.

points: A currency regime is a spectrum, not a binary: fixed/pegged at one end, freely floating at the other, and a managed float in between, where the market sets the day-to-day rate but the central bank smooths excessive volatility.
India runs a managed float. The RBI does not defend a specific USD/INR level; it intervenes in the spot, forward and, since 2020, offshore NDF markets to reduce disorderly swings.

The impossible trinity explains why regime choice is constrained: a country can have at most two of a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy. India chose a managed float and independent rate-setting over a fully open capital account.

India's rupee moved from a colonial-era peg to the British pound, through a currency-basket peg and a 1991 balance of payments crisis, to a unified market-determined rate from 1993 onward, the managed float still in place today.
Formal inflation targeting since 2016 gives the RBI a clear domestic mandate that it can pursue precisely because it is not obligated to defend a fixed rupee level at any cost.
